title: Full-Spectrum Graph Neural Networks: Expressive and Scalable
one_liner: To learn complex graph patterns, treat pairs of connected nodes as the unit, not single nodes, and filter them by both eigenvalue pairs instead of one.
lead: Graph neural networks learn relationships between connected items (like atoms in a molecule or friends in a social network). Standard versions see only one item at a time. This paper lifts that view: see two connected items together, then filter them by patterns of connection pairs, not connection singles. This catches patterns the old way missed.

problem.h2: Standard graph networks see one item at a time
paras: A graph is a web of items (nodes) connected by lines (edges). A social network has people (nodes) and friendships (edges). A molecule has atoms (nodes) and chemical bonds (edges). A standard graph neural network looks at each node alone—what is it connected to?—and learns a pattern. But real graphs hide patterns that live in *pairs* of nodes. For example, one person is friends with both a musician and a banker: the *pair* (musician, banker) matters because they shape each other's influence through that mutual friend. The old method sees each friend separately and misses this.

A beginner might try: add more layers, look further out. But that does not solve it. The old math (called the Weisfeiler-Lehman test) proves there is a hard ceiling: single-node views cannot see all pair patterns. The network gets stuck.

callout.html: Instead of filtering each node by its connection strength, filter each pair of nodes by the strength pattern of their connection pair.

steps.text: Calculate which pair-patterns are strong or weak in the graph (eigenvalues of connections between connections).

Combine the filtered pair signals to update what each node learns.

object.h2: What changes: from nodes to pairs
paras: The paper moves the focus from single nodes to pairs of nodes. Where the old method asked, 'What does node A see?', the new method asks, 'What does the pair (A, B) see together?' This is the single object being changed.

hidden.name: pair-pattern expressivity
paras: Node-pair expressivity is the set of all distinct pair patterns the network can learn to distinguish. A graph has many pair patterns: pairs that form triangles, pairs that bridge two distant regions, pairs of nodes with matching degrees. Old networks were mathematically blocked from seeing all of them. The new method measures how many of these patterns it can now distinguish.

The paper proves mathematically that FSpecGNNs can universally approximate node-pair signals, meaning they can learn any relationship between a pair of nodes if given the right tuning. This is measured by comparing what substructure-counting tasks (like counting triangles or bipartite shapes) the network can solve.

heat.caption: Darker means the network can now see and distinguish this pair pattern; lighter means the old network could not.

reads.html: The network can now tell apart triangles, X-shapes, and other substructures because it looks at connected pairs, not single nodes.
Full-Spectrum GNNs universally approximate node-pair signals and break the Weisfeiler-Lehman expressivity ceiling.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: pair-based filtering captures what single nodes miss
paras: A spectral filter is a formula that assigns a strength to each piece of information based on its frequency or pattern. In the old way, each node gets one spectral filter based on one eigenvalue (a measure of how patterns flow through the graph). In the new way, each pair of nodes gets a filter based two eigenvalues simultaneously. Why does this matter? Because some patterns only show up when you look at two things together. For example, a triangle has a pair pattern (node B and node C are both connected to node A) that cannot be detected by looking at A, B, and C separately. The old method counts each node and misses the shape.

The paper also proves this mathematically. A theorem (the Weisfeiler-Lehman test) says single-node networks can never catch all patterns—there is a hard ceiling built into the math. Pair-node networks break that ceiling because they see a richer input: not just what node A connects to, but how node A's neighbors relate to each other. Two separate eyes see more than one eye alone.

math.words: The output at each pair is the original pair signal multiplied by the sum of two spectral filters, each one applied to one eigenvalue of the pair-connection matrix.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Pair (Node A, Node B): signal is 0.8 (moderately connected).
First eigenvalue lambda1 = 2.0 (strong main pattern), filter1(2.0) = 0.9.
Contrast: if the pair had lambda2 = 2.0 instead, filter2(2.0) = 0.9, sum = 1.8, output = 1.44—a markedly different signal for a different pair pattern.

math.note: Both eigenvalues shape the pair together; the network learns to weight them differently for different kinds of structures.

charts.title: Old method (single-node filter)
charts.note: Single nodes excel at local tasks but fail on pair patterns.

charts.title: FSpecGNN (pair-based filter)
charts.note: Pairs handle both structure and local tasks, with no blind spot.

items.html: Computing for every pair of nodes can explode in cost. The paper uses a low-rank approximation (polynomial filters instead of full bivariate) to keep it fast, but if the graph has millions of edges, this still becomes slow.

items.b: Pair patterns may be sparse in the data.
items.html: If the true pattern lives at the pair level but the training data rarely shows that pair, the network may not learn it.
The method must decide which pairs to filter (edges, or arbitrary node pairs?). Different choices break different tasks.
For graphs with clear pair structure (molecule bonds, graph algorithms) and moderate size, FSpecGNN with low-rank approximation succeeds consistently.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny graph with a known structure (e.g., a ring of triangles or a bipartite graph) and train FSpecGNN to count substructures. Compare the accuracy on substructure counting against an old spectral GNN. The pair-based method should get close to 100% on triangles and bipartite shapes; the old method should fail. Measure accuracy on different substructure types to show the expressivity gain.
demo.closing: The demo must show FSpecGNN scoring near 100% on triangle counting while the old method scores below 50%—proof that pair vision unlocks structure the node view cannot see.
